The Mamluk Sultanate. From 1250 to 1517 of the common era, this was a unique military state ruled by mamluks—enslaved soldiers of Caucasian or Central Asian origin who were trained as warriors and rose to supreme power in Egypt and the Levant. Though built on the paradox of slave rule, the Mamluks became one of history's most effective and enduring military regimes, defending Islam against both the Mongols and the Crusaders while patronizing magnificent art and architecture.

The Mamluks originated as the Bahri, or River, Mamluk faction, a military caste within the Ayyubid army who seized power from the last Ayyubid sultan in 1250. Two early Mamluk sultans, Qutuz and Baybars, defeated the Mongol Ilkhanate at the Battle of Ain Jalut in 1260, preventing Mongol conquest of Egypt and earning immense prestige across the Islamic world. They ruled Egypt, the Levant, and the Hijaz, including the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, making them custodians of Islam's holiest sites and spiritual authorities even when rivals claimed the caliphate. The Mamluks operated a meritocratic military system where ambitious mamluks could rise from slavery to sultanate through martial skill and political acumen, creating competitive incentives for capable commanders. They patronized elaborate Islamic architecture, decorative arts, calligraphy, and urban development. The Citadel of Cairo and numerous mosques and madrasas from this era remain iconic. They maintained control for over 250 years despite persistent internal power struggles and assassinations. Finally they were overthrown by the expanding Ottoman Empire in 1517.

The Ayyubid dynasty was the regime they replaced in Egypt. The Ottoman Empire was the Turkish power that conquered them. The Battle of Ain Jalut stood as their defining military victory. And Mecca was one of the holy cities under their protection and stewardship.
